newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundians remember murdered Catholic archbishop.
newsitem.headline: Burundians remember murdered Catholic archbishop.

text.p: Burundians were called upon to mourn on Tuesday the country's top Catholic churchman, Archbishop Joachim Ruhuna, who was murdered over a week ago.
Ruhuna and two nuns died when they were ambushed, apparently by rebels, and although one of the nuns has been buried the bodies of the archbishop and the other nun have not been recovered.
Four people travelling with them survived the attack north of Gitega, the second largest city in the tiny central African country rent by civil war between ethnic Hutu rebels and the Tutsi-led army.

The Catholic church called a solemn mass in Gitega and state radio said civil servants had been asked to attend memorial services for Ruhuna, the most senior cleric to be killed in the fiercely Catholic country in three years of fighting.

Hutu rebel leader Leonard Nyangoma was one of five members of the Hutu-dominated Frodebu party who announced on Monday they were taking control of the party and backed armed struggle against the government of Tutsi strongman Pierre Buyoya.

President Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, a member of Frodebu, has sheltered in the U.S. embassy in the capital since shortly before Buyoya took power in a July 25 coup. The deposed president's signature did not appear on Monday's statement.
Regional states quickly imposed sanctions after the coup in an effort to force Buyoya to talk to rebels.
Fears are widespread that Burundi might go the way of its northern neighbour Rwanda, where up to a million people were killed in genocide and three months of civil war in 1994.
The countries have a similar ethnic mix -- overwhelming Hutu majorities with around 15 percent of their populations made up of Tutsis.
The Frodebu party won democratic polls in 1993 but the elected Hutu president was assassinated by Tutsi troops, triggering massacres of an estimated 50,000 Tutsis and Hutus across the country.

Buyoya, who says he is more of a democrat than his rivals, has said his military-appointed government will rule for a transitional period of three years. Last week he lifted bans on political parties and parliament imposed after he seized power.
His main Tutsi rival, Jean-Baptiste Bagaza, said on Tuesday that unless there were talks, killings would continue to tear the country apart.
"Before the rebels just had machetes. Now they have mortars. Next year they will have more," he said.
